cps.text: Some economic historians ______ that late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century households in the United States experienced an economy of scale when it came to food purchases—they assumed that large households spent less on food per person than did small households.

cps.text: Ecologist Exequiel Ezcurra and colleagues found that the inhabitants of the Mexica empire used natural landmarks to track time with a high degree of ______.
cps.label: I

cps.text: By observing the sun’s position in relation to various points on the mountains surrounding the Basin of Mexico, the Mexica were able to precisely identify the dates when significant events such as solstices occurred.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In editor Lisa Yaszek’s introduction to her anthology The Future Is Female! More Classic Science Fiction Stories by Women, Yaszek identifies an increasing sense of ______ feminist mode of writing in the 1970s,
cps.label: C

cps.text: in contrast to many woman-authored science fiction stories of the 1920s to 1960s whose politics were less deliberately signaled.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: For a 2020 exhibition, photographer and neurobiologist Okunola Jeyifous ______ a series of new images based on a series of alphabet posters from the 1970s known as the “Black ABCs,” which featured Black children from Chicago.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Jeyifous photographed the now-adult models and layered the photos over magnified images of the models’ cells,
cps.label: I

cps.text: resulting in what he called “micro and macro portraiture.”
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Diego Velázquez was the leading artist in the court of King Philip IV of Spain during the seventeenth century,
cps.label: I

cps.text: but his influence was hardly ______ Spain: realist and impressionist painters around the world employed his techniques and echoed elements of his style.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Birds sing to communicate over potentially great distances.
cps.label: I

cps.text: For this reason, many researchers believe that birds in densely vegetated habitats generally sing at lower frequencies than birds living in comparatively sparse habitats,
cps.label: C

cps.text: since dense vegetation tends to ______ the distance that high-frequency sounds can travel.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In 1776, the United States sent Benjamin Franklin to France to try to win the country’s support in the United States’ fight for independence from Great Britain.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Franklin was very popular in France.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This ______ surely helped him to convince France to assist the United States.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The artisans of the Igun Eronmwon guild in Benin City, Nigeria, typically ______ the bronze- and brass-casting techniques that have been passed down through their families since the thirteenth century,
cps.label: I

cps.text: but they don’t strictly observe every tradition;
cps.label: I

cps.text: for example, guild members now use air-conditioning motors instead of handheld bellows to help heat their forges.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Public policy researcher Anthony Fowler studied the history of elections in Australia, a country that requires citizens to vote.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Fowler argues that requiring citizens to vote leads to a significant increase in voters who would otherwise not have the time or motivation to vote.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Thus, election results in countries that require citizens to vote better reflect the preferences of the country as a whole.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Governments in democratic countries function better when more people vote.
cps.label: C

cps.text: However, forcing people to vote may have negative consequences.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Shane P. Singh and Jason Roy studied what happens when a country requires its citizens to vote.
cps.label: I

cps.text: They found that when people feel forced to vote, they tend to spend less time looking for information about their choices when voting.
cps.label: I

cps.text: As a result, votes from these voters may not reflect their actual preferences.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Italian painters in the 1500s rarely depicted themselves in their work.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Even more rare were self-portrait paintings that portrayed the artist as a painter.
cps.label: I

cps.text: At the time, painting was not yet respected as a profession, so painters mostly chose to emphasize other qualities in their self-portraits, like their intellect or social status.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In the city of Bologna, the first artist to depict themself painting was a man named Annibale Carracci.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A painting of his from around 1585 shows Carracci in front of an easel holding a palette.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In their self-portraits, Bolognese artists typically avoided referring to the act of painting until the mid-1600s.
cps.label: I

cps.text: However, Lavinia Fontana’s 1577 painting, Self-Portrait at the Keyboard, stands out as the earliest example of such a work by an artist from Bologna.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Although the artist is depicted playing music, in the background, one can spot a painting easel by a window.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Dance choreographer Alvin Ailey’s deep admiration for jazz music can most clearly be felt in the rhythms and beats his works were set to.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Ailey collaborated with some of the greatest jazz legends, like Charles Mingus, Charlie Parker, and perhaps his favorite, Duke Ellington.
cps.label: I

cps.text: With his choice of music, Ailey helped bring jazz to life for his audiences.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Jazz is present throughout Ailey’s work, but it’s most visible in Ailey’s approach to choreography.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Ailey often incorporated improvisation, a signature characteristic of jazz music, in his work.
cps.label: I

cps.text: When managing his dance company, Ailey rarely forced his dancers to an exact set of specific moves.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Instead, he encouraged his dancers to let their own skills and experiences shape their performances, as jazz musicians do.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Historians studying pre-Inca Peru have looked to ceramic vessels to understand daily life among the Moche people.
cps.label: I

cps.text: These mold-made sculptures present plants, animals, and human faces in precise ways—vessels representing human faces are so detailed that scholars have interpreted facial markings to represent scars and other skin irregularities.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Some historians have even used these objects to identify potential skin diseases that may have afflicted people at the time.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Art historian and archaeologist Lisa Trever has argued that the interpretation of Moche “portrait” vessels as hyper-realistic portrayals of identifiable people may inadvertently disregard the creativity of the objects’ creators.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Moche ceramic vessels, Trever argues, are artworks in which sculptors could free their imagination, using realistic objects and people around them as inspiration to explore more abstract concepts.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Today the starchy root cassava is found in many dishes across West Africa, but its rise to popularity was slow.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Portuguese traders brought cassava from Brazil to the West African coast in the 1500s.
cps.label: I

cps.text: But at this time, people living in the capitals further inland had little contact with coastal communities.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Thus, cassava remained relatively unknown to most of the region’s inhabitants until the 1800s.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Cassava’s slow adoption into the diet of West Africans is mainly due to the nature of the crop itself.
cps.label: C

cps.text: If not cooked properly, cassava can be toxic.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Knowledge of how to properly prepare cassava needed to spread before the food could grow in popularity.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The arrival of formerly enslaved people from Brazil in the 1800s, who brought their knowledge of cassava and its preparation with them, thus directly fueled the spread of this crop.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Flamingos are known for their vibrant pink coloring, but they’re actually born with gray feathers.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Their pink color comes from eating brine shrimp, but brine shrimp aren’t naturally pink either.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Animals can’t produce carotenoids, the pigments that provide the pink hue.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The algae that brine shrimp feed on, however, can produce these pigments.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Thus, the pinker the flamingo, the more shrimp it has eaten.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Ecologist Juan Amat has found that flamingos apply a kind of makeup to make themselves appear pinker.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A gland near their tail contains pigments that come from the food they eat.
cps.label: I

cps.text: When the flamingos groom themselves using the pigments, their feathers become pinker.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Flamingos may do this to improve their success during mating season, when they would benefit from looking pinker.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Most scientists agree that the moon was likely formed after a collision between Earth and a large planet named Theia.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This collision likely created a huge debris field, made up of material from both Earth and Theia.
cps.label: I

cps.text: On April 26th, 1777, Sybil Ludington rode 40 miles by horse through Putnam County, New York, to gather up local militia.
cps.label: I

cps.text: British forces were burning nearby Danbury, Connecticut, and Ludington wanted to rally rebel troops to meet them.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Although she was only 16 years old at the time, her brave feat made Ludington one of the heroes of the American Revolution.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Since then, Ludington has been widely celebrated, inspiring postage stamps, statues, and even children’s TV series.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Historian Paula D. Hunt researched the life and legacy of Sybil Ludington but found no evidence for her famous ride.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Although many articles and books have been written about Ludington, Hunt believes writers may have been inventing details about Ludington as they retold her story.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Ludington is revered by Americans today, but there simply isn’t a strong historical record of her heroic ride.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: For decades, bluegrass musicians have debated whether their genre should exclude influences from mainstream genres such as rock.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Many insist that bluegrass is defined by its adherence to the folk music of the US South, out of which bluegrass emerged.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Such “purists,” as they are known, regard the recordings of Bill Monroe, which established the bluegrass sound in the 1940s, as a standard against which the genre should still be measured.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In reality, Bill Monroe created the bluegrass sound in the 1940s by combining Southern folk music with commercial genres that had arisen only a few decades before, such as jazz and the blues.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Since bluegrass has always been a mixed genre, contemporary bluegrass musicians should not be forbidden from incorporating into it influences from rock and other mainstream genres.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Literary scholars have struggled with the vastness of Nigerian writer Wole Soyinka’s collective works of drama (spanning over 20 plays in total).
cps.label: C

cps.text: It is best, however, to understand Soyinka’s body of work as a dramatist chronologically.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Soyinka’s progression as a playwright can be considered to fall into three periods, with each one representing a particular thematic and stylistic cohesion: the 1960s, the two decades between 1970 and 1990, and lastly, from roughly 1990 onwards.
cps.label: I

cps.text: However, critics who have considered Soyinka’s plays to fit neatly into three phases overlook potential commonalities in Soyinka’s work that span across these phases.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Additionally, this view may discount significant differences in the styles and content of plays written around the same time.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In a study of insect behavior, Samadi Galpayage and colleagues presented bumblebees with small wooden balls and observed many of the bees clinging to, rolling, and dragging the objects.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The researchers provided no external rewards (such as food) to encourage these interactions.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The bees simply appeared to be playing—and for no other reason than because they were having fun.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Insects do not have cortexes or other brain areas associated with emotions in humans.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Still, Galpayage and her team have shown that bumblebees may engage in play, possibly experiencing some kind of positive emotional state.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Other studies have suggested that bees experience negative emotional states (for example, stress), but as Galpayage and her team have acknowledged, emotions in insects, if they do indeed exist, are likely very rudimentary.
cps.label: C

cps.text: American sculptor Edmonia Lewis is best known for her sculptures that represent figures from history and mythology, such as The Death of Cleopatra and Hagar.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Although Lewis sculpted other subjects, her career as a sculptor is best represented by the works in which she depicted these historical and mythical themes.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Art historians have typically ignored the many portrait busts Edmonia Lewis created.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Lewis likely carved these busts (sculptures of a person’s head) frequently throughout her long career.
cps.label: I

cps.text: She is known for her sculptures that represent historical figures, but Lewis likely supported herself financially by carving portrait busts for acquaintances who paid her to represent their features.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Thus, Lewis’s portrait busts are a central aspect of her career as a sculptor.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Some animal species, like the leopard, can be found in many kinds of areas.
cps.label: I

cps.text: On the other hand, tropical mountain bird species tend to be limited in the types of spaces they can call home.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This is because many mountain bird species are only able to survive at very specific elevations.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Over time, these species have likely become used to living at a specific temperature.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Therefore, these species struggle to survive at elevations that are warmer or colder than they are used to.
cps.label: C

cps.text: A new study reviewed observations of nearly 3,000 bird species to understand why tropical mountain bird species live at specific elevations.
cps.label: I

cps.text: They noted that when a mountain bird species was found in an area with many other bird species, it tended to inhabit much smaller geographic areas.
cps.label: I

cps.text: It is thus likely that competition for resources with other species, not temperature, limits where these birds can live.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Although food writing is one of the most widely read genres in the United States, literary scholars have long neglected it.
cps.label: C

cps.text: And within this genre, cookbooks attract the least scholarly attention of all, regardless of how well written they may be.
cps.label: C

cps.text: This is especially true of works dedicated to regional US cuisines, whose complexity and historical significance are often overlooked.
cps.label: C

cps.text: With her 1976 cookbook The Taste of Country Cooking, Edna Lewis popularized the refined Southern cooking she had grown up with in Freetown, an all-Black community in Virginia.
cps.label: I

cps.text: She also set a new standard for cookbook writing: the recipes and memoir passages interspersing them are written in prose more elegant than that of most novels.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Yet despite its inarguable value as a piece of writing, Lewis’s masterpiece has received almost no attention from literary scholars.
cps.label: C

cps.text: She crossed the woods she knew so well.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The trees seemed to extend their branches like welcoming arms.
cps.label: C

cps.text: They greeted her as an old friend.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Soon she reached the river-side.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: A team led by Bernardo Strassburg has found that rewilding farmland (returning the land to its natural state) could help preserve biodiversity and offset carbon emissions.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The amount of farmland that would need to be restored, they found, is remarkably low.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Rewilding a mere 15% of the world’s current farmland would prevent 60% of expected species extinctions and help absorb nearly 299 gigatons of carbon dioxide—a clear win in the fight against the biodiversity and climate crises.
cps.label: C

cps.text: While Strassburg’s team’s findings certainly offer encouraging insight into the potential benefits of rewilding, it’s important to consider potential effects on global food supplies.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The researchers suggest that to compensate for the loss of food-producing land, remaining farmland would need to produce even more food.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Thus, policies focused on rewilding farmland must also address strategies for higher-yield farming.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Historians Tiya Miles and Roy E. Finkenbine have both documented the assistance Indigenous peoples gave to Black freedom seekers leaving the South before the US Civil War.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Much of the historical evidence of this help comes from Indigenous oral traditions and from autobiographies written by the freedom seekers.
cps.label: I

cps.text: One such narrative is Jermain Loguen’s autobiography, which tells about how Neshnabé (Potawatomi) villagers offered him food, lodging, and directions during his 1835 journey from Tennessee to Canada.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Ordinary soap bubbles usually exist for a minute or less before popping due to either a rupture forced by gravity-induced drainage or the evaporation of the liquid from which the bubble is composed.
cps.label: I

cps.text: But physicist Aymeric Roux and colleagues discovered ways to mitigate these factors, resulting in bubbles that can last for a year or more.
cps.label: I

cps.text: For example, glycerol tends to adhere to water molecules, so a bubble with a shell that contains both water and glycerol is able to draw additional water molecules from the surrounding air and thereby compensate for evaporation.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Researchers have found a nearly 164,000-year-old molar from a member of the archaic human species known as Denisovans in a cave in Laos, suggesting that Denisovans lived in a wider range of environments than indicated by earlier evidence.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Before the discovery, Denisovans were thought to have lived only at high altitudes in relatively cold climates in what are now Russia and China, but the discovery of the tooth in Laos suggests that they may have lived at low altitudes in relatively warm climates in Southeast Asia as well.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In 2007, computer scientist Luis von Ahn was working on converting printed books into a digital format.
cps.label: I

cps.text: He found that some words were distorted enough that digital scanners couldn’t recognize them, but most humans could easily read them.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Composer Florence Price won first place for her score Symphony in E Minor at the 1932 Wanamaker Foundation Awards.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The piece was performed the following year by the Chicago Symphony Orchestra, a significant recognition of its quality.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Price continued to compose many musical pieces throughout her career, blending traditional Black spirituals with classical European Romantic musical traditions.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In recent years, Price’s concertos and symphonies have been performed and recorded by several major orchestras, further preserving her work for others to enjoy.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Fanny’s friends did not interest Polly much; she was rather afraid of them [because] they seemed so much older and wiser than herself, even those younger in years.
cps.label: I

cps.text: They talked about things of which she knew nothing and when Fanny tried to explain, she didn’t find them interesting; indeed, some of them rather shocked and puzzled her.
cps.label: C

cps.text: San Francisco is known for the colorful murals painted on many of its buildings.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The densest collection of murals is found on Balmy Alley in the Mission District neighborhood.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In the 1970s, Latina artists painted vivid scenes of community life on walls along this block.
cps.label: I

cps.text: As the original murals have faded, later generations of artists have painted new ones over them.
cps.label: I

cps.text: As a result, Balmy Alley has become a living showcase of San Francisco’s artistic spirit, with its murals reflecting changes in the cultural life of the city.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Some bird species don’t raise their own chicks.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Instead, adult females lay their eggs in other nests, next to another bird species’ own eggs.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Female cuckoos have been seen quickly laying eggs in the nests of other bird species when those birds are out looking for food.
cps.label: I

cps.text: After the eggs hatch, the noncuckoo parents will typically raise the cuckoo chicks as if they were their own offspring, even if the cuckoos look very different from the other chicks.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Go forth, my son, Winged by my heart’s desire!
cps.label: C

cps.text: Great reaches, yet unknown, Await For your possession.
cps.label: I

cps.text: I may not, if I would, Retrace the way with you, My pilgrimage is through,
cps.label: C

cps.text: But life is calling you!

cps.text: People whose desire is solely for self-realisation never know where they are going.
cps.label: C

cps.text: They can’t know.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In one sense of the word it is of course necessary to know oneself: that is the first achievement of knowledge.
cps.label: I

cps.text: But to recognise that the soul of a man is unknowable, is the ultimate achievement of wisdom.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The final mystery is oneself.
cps.label: C

cps.text: When one has weighed the sun in the balance, and measured the steps of the moon, and mapped out the seven heavens star by star, there still remains oneself.

cps.text: Who can calculate the orbit of his own soul?

cps.text: Theresa Cole and her team argue that penguins could fly at some point, but that they lost that ability more than 60 million years ago as they adapted to marine life.
cps.label: C

cps.text: After examining various penguin fossils and genetic information, the researchers concluded that over time penguins developed underwater vision, blood oxygenation, and bone density better suited for swimming than flying.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Thus, environmental conditions might have driven penguins to change from flyers to swimmers.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: More than two years ago my parents bought a piano from some people who were moving to Utah.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Mom and Dad gave it to my brothers and me for Christmas.
cps.label: I

cps.text: I had to act really happy because it was such a big present, but I pretty much hated the thing from the second it was carried into the hallway upstairs, which is right next to my bedroom.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The piano glared at me.
cps.label: C

cps.text: It was like a songbird in a cage.
cps.label: C

cps.text: It wanted to be set free.

cps.text: In most building demolitions, the building materials are destroyed and sent to landfills.
cps.label: I

cps.text: City officials in Portland, Oregon, wanted to reduce this waste.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The officials passed a law requiring demolition companies to deconstruct some buildings instead.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Deconstruction involves carefully taking buildings apart piece by piece.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Damage to the materials is avoided so that they can be reused in new constructions.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A 2019 study found that 27 percent of materials from deconstructions in Portland were able to be reused.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The remaining materials were processed for recycling instead of going to a landfill.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The strip tells the story of Torchy, a young woman who leaves Mississippi to become a performer in New York City.

cps.text: Unfortunately, risk evaluations based on nanohybrids’ constituents are not reliable: conjugation may alter constituents’ physiochemical properties such that innocuous nanomaterials form a nanohybrid that is anything but.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The potential for enhanced toxicity of nanohybrids relative to the toxicity of constituent nanomaterials has drawn deserved attention, but the effects of nanomaterial conjugation vary by case.
cps.label: C

cps.text: For instance, it was recently shown that a nanohybrid of silicon dioxide and zinc oxide preserved the desired optical transparency of zinc oxide nanoparticles while mitigating the nanoparticles’ potential to damage DNA.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Astronomer Mark Holland and colleagues examined four white dwarfs—small, dense remnants of past stars—in order to determine the composition of exoplanets that used to orbit those stars.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Studying wavelengths of light in the white dwarf atmospheres, the team reported that traces of elements such as lithium and sodium support the presence of exoplanets with continental crusts similar to Earth’s.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Past studies of white dwarf atmospheres have concluded that certain exoplanets had continental crusts.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Geologist Keith Putirka and astronomer Siyi Xu argue that those studies unduly emphasize atmospheric traces of lithium and other individual elements as signifiers of the types of rock found on Earth.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The studies don’t adequately account for different minerals made up of various ratios of those elements, and the possibility of rock types not found on Earth that contain those minerals.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Africa’s Sahara region—once a lush ecosystem—began to dry out about 8,000 years ago.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A change in Earth’s orbit that affected climate has been posited as a cause of desertification, but archaeologist David Wright also attributes the shift to Neolithic peoples.
cps.label: C

cps.text: He cites their adoption of pastoralism as a factor in the region drying out: the pastoralists’ livestock depleted vegetation, prompting the events that created the Sahara Desert.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Research by Chris Brierley et al. challenges the idea that Neolithic peoples contributed to the Sahara’s desertification.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Using a climate-vegetation model, the team concluded that the end of the region’s humid period occurred 500 years earlier than previously assumed.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The timing suggests that Neolithic peoples didn’t exacerbate aridity in the region but, in fact, may have helped delay environmental changes with practices (e.g., selective grazing) that preserved vegetation.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Soy sauce, made from fermented soybeans, is noted for its umami flavor.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Umami—one of the five basic tastes along with sweet, bitter, salty, and sour—was formally classified when its taste receptors were discovered in the 2000s.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In 2007, to define the pure umami flavor scientists Rie Ishii and Michael O’Mahony used broths made from shiitake mushrooms and kombu seaweed, and two panels of Japanese and US judges closely agreed on a description of the taste.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A 2022 experiment by Manon Jünger et al. led to a greater understanding of soy sauce’s flavor profile.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The team initially presented a mixture of compounds with low molecular weights to taste testers who found it was not as salty or bitter as real soy sauce.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Further analysis of soy sauce identified proteins, including dipeptides, that enhanced umami flavor and also contributed to saltiness.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The team then made a mix of 50 chemical compounds that re-created soy sauce’s flavor.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Mycoprotein is a fungal biomass that can be eaten as an alternative to meat.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Studies of the environmental impact of its manufacture generally agree it is lower than that of beef and closer to that of chicken or pork.
cps.label: C

cps.text: But the expense of producing mycoprotein restricts its availability to a few countries with postindustrial economies.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Knowing that cost reductions would expand access to mycoprotein, biochemists are exploring solutions, such as a cheaper substrate to feed the mycoprotein as it grows.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Cattle farming is a principal cause of global deforestation, and a study by Florian Humpenöder and his colleagues found that replacing 20% of beef consumption worldwide with consumption of mycoprotein would cut deforestation by half if accomplished over the next thirty years.
cps.label: C

cps.text: However, this would likely involve only a small change in agricultural water consumption, since water once dedicated to raising cattle would be diverted to raising crops instead.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Fossils of the hominin Australopithecus africanus have been found in the Sterkfontein Caves of South Africa, but assigning an age to the fossils is challenging because of the unreliability of dating methods in this context.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The geology of Sterkfontein has caused soil layers from different periods to mix, impeding stratigraphic dating, and dates cannot be reliably imputed from those of nearby animal bones since the bones may have been relocated by flooding.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Archaeologists used new cosmogenic nuclide dating techniques to reevaluate the ages of A. africanus fossils found in the Sterkfontein Caves.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This technique involves analyzing the cosmogenic nucleotides in the breccia—the matrix of rock fragments immediately surrounding the fossils.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The researchers assert that this approach avoids the potential for misdating associated with assigning ages based on Sterkfontein’s soil layers or animal bones.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Like the work of Ralph Ellison before her, Toni Morrison’s novels feature scenes in which characters deliver sermons of such length and verbal dexterity that for a time, the text exchanges the formal parameters of fiction for those of oral literature.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Given the many other echoes of Ellison in Morrison’s novels, both in structure and prose style, these scenes suggest Ellison’s direct influence on Morrison.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In their destabilizing effect on literary form, the sermons in Morrison’s works recall those in Ellison’s.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Yet literature by Black Americans abounds in moments where interpolated speech erodes the division between oral and written forms that literature in English has traditionally observed.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Morrison’s use of the sermon is attributable not only to the influence of Ellison but also to a community-wide strategy of resistance to externally imposed literary conventions.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Films and television shows commonly include a long list of credits naming the people involved in a production.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Credit sequences may not be exciting, but they generally ensure that everyone’s contributions are duly acknowledged.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Because they are highly standardized, film and television credits are also valuable to anyone researching the careers of pioneering cast and crew members who have worked in the mediums.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Video game scholars face a major challenge in the industry’s failure to consistently credit the artists, designers, and other contributors involved in making video games.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Without a reliable record of which people worked on which games, questions about the medium’s development can be difficult to answer, and the accomplishments of all but its best-known innovators can be difficult to trace.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The Cretaceous-Paleogene (K-Pg) mass extinction event is usually attributed solely to an asteroid impact near Chicxulub, Mexico.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Some scientists argue that volcanic activity was the true cause, as the K-Pg event occurred relatively early in a long period of eruption of the Deccan Traps range that initially produced huge amounts of climate-altering gases.
cps.label: C

cps.text: These dissenters note that other mass extinctions have coincided with large volcanic eruptions, while only the K-Pg event lines up with an asteroid strike.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In a 2020 study, Pincelli Hull and her colleagues analyzed ocean core samples and modeled climate changes around the K-Pg event.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The team concluded that Deccan Traps gases did affect global conditions prior to the event, but that the climate returned to normal well before the extinctions began—extinctions that instead closely align with the Chicxulub impact.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Virginia Woolf’s 1928 novel Orlando is an oddity within her body of work.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Her other major novels consist mainly of scenes of everyday life and describe their characters’ interior states in great detail, whereas Orlando propels itself through a series of fantastical events and considers its characters’ psychology more superficially.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Woolf herself sometimes regarded the novel as a minor work, even admitting once that she “began it as a joke.”
cps.label: C

cps.text: Like Woolf’s other great novels, Orlando portrays how people’s memories inform their experience of the present.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Like those works, it examines how people navigate social interactions shaped by gender and social class.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Though it is lighter in tone—more entertaining, even—this literary “joke” nonetheless engages seriously with the themes that motivated the four or five other novels by Woolf that have achieved the status of literary classics.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Most animals can regenerate some parts of their bodies, such as skin.
cps.label: I

cps.text: But when a three-banded panther worm is cut into three pieces, each piece grows into a new worm.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Researchers are investigating this feat partly to learn more about humans’ comparatively limited abilities to regenerate, and they’re making exciting progress.
cps.label: I

cps.text: An especially promising discovery is that both humans and panther worms have a gene for early growth response (EGR) linked to regeneration.
cps.label: I

cps.text: When Mansi Srivastava and her team reported that panther worms, like humans, possess a gene for EGR, it caused excitement.
cps.label: I

cps.text: However, as the team pointed out, the gene likely functions very differently in humans than it does in panther worms.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Srivastava has likened EGR to a switch that activates other genes involved in regeneration in panther worms, but how this switch operates in humans remains unclear.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Conventional wisdom long held that human social systems evolved in stages, beginning with hunter-gatherers forming small bands of members with roughly equal status.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The shift to agriculture about 12,000 years ago sparked population growth that led to the emergence of groups with hierarchical structures: associations of clans first, then chiefdoms, and finally, bureaucratic states.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In a 2021 book, anthropologist David Graeber and archaeologist David Wengrow maintain that humans have always been socially flexible, alternately forming systems based on hierarchy and collective ones with decentralized leadership.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The authors point to evidence that as far back as 50,000 years ago some hunter-gatherers adjusted their social structures seasonally, at times dispersing in small groups but also assembling into communities that included esteemed individuals.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Despite its beautiful prose, The Guns of August, Barbara Tuchman’s 1962 analysis of the start of World War I, has certain weaknesses as a work of history.
cps.label: C

cps.text: It fails to address events in Eastern Europe just before the outbreak of hostilities, thereby giving the impression that Germany was the war’s principal instigator.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Had Tuchman consulted secondary works available to her by scholars such as Luigi Albertini, she would not have neglected the influence of events in Eastern Europe on Germany’s actions.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Barbara Tuchman’s The Guns of August is an engrossing if dated introduction to World War I.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Tuchman’s analysis of primary documents is laudable, but her main thesis that European powers committed themselves to a catastrophic outcome by refusing to deviate from military plans developed prior to the conflict is implausibly reductive.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In 2007, a team led by Alice Storey analyzed a chicken bone found in El Arenal, Chile, dating it to 1321–1407 CE—over a century before Europeans invaded the region, bringing their own chickens.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Storey also found that the El Arenal chicken shared a unique genetic mutation with the ancient chicken breeds of the Polynesian Islands in the Pacific.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Thus, Polynesian peoples, not later Europeans, probably first introduced chickens to South America.
cps.label: C

cps.text: An Australian research team weakened the case for a Polynesian origin for the El Arenal chicken by confirming that the mutation identified by Storey has occurred in breeds from around the world.
cps.label: C

cps.text: More recently, though, a team led by Agusto Luzuriaga-Neira found that South American chicken breeds and Polynesian breeds share other genetic markers that European breeds lack.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Thus, the preponderance of evidence now favors a Polynesian origin.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Ecologists have long wondered how thousands of microscopic phytoplankton species can live together near ocean surfaces competing for the same resources.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The fossil record suggests that mammoths went extinct around 11 thousand years (kyr) ago.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In a 2021 study of environmental DNA (eDNA)—genetic material shed into the environment by organisms—in the Arctic, Yucheng Wang and colleagues found mammoth eDNA in sedimentary layers formed millennia later, around 4 kyr ago.
cps.label: I

cps.text: To account for this discrepancy, Joshua H. Miller and Carl Simpson proposed that arctic temperatures could preserve a mammoth carcass on the surface, allowing it to leach DNA into the environment, for several thousand years.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Wang and colleagues concede that eDNA contains DNA from both living organisms and carcasses, but for DNA to leach from remains over several millennia requires that the remains be perpetually on the surface.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Scavengers and weathering in the Arctic, however, are likely to break down surface remains well before a thousand years have passed.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Many computer animators prioritize this question as they strive to create ever more realistic environments and lighting.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Generally, while characters in computer-animated films appear highly exaggerated, environments and lighting are carefully engineered to mimic reality.
cps.label: I

cps.text: But some animators, such as Pixar’s Sanjay Patel, are focused on a different question.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Rather than asking first whether the environments and lighting they’re creating are convincingly lifelike, Patel and others are asking whether these elements reflect their films’ unique stories.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Dominique Potvin and colleagues captured five Australian magpies (Gymnorhina tibicen) to test a new design for attaching tracking devices to birds.
cps.label: I

cps.text: As the researchers fitted each magpie with a tracker attached by a small harness, they noticed some magpies without trackers pecking at another magpie’s tracker until it broke off.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The researchers suggest that this behavior could be evidence of magpies attempting to help another magpie without benefiting themselves.
cps.label: C

cps.text: It can be tempting to think that animals are deliberately providing help when we see them removing trackers and other equipment from one another, especially when a species is known to exhibit other cooperative behaviors.
cps.label: C

cps.text: At the same time, it can be difficult to exclude the possibility that individuals are simply interested in the equipment because of its novelty, curiously pawing or pecking at it until it detaches.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The field of study called affective neuroscience seeks instinctive, physiological causes for feelings such as pleasure or displeasure.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Because these sensations are linked to a chemical component (for example, the release of the neurotransmitter dopamine in the brain when one receives or expects a reward), they can be said to have a partly physiological basis.
cps.label: I

cps.text: These processes have been described in mammals, but Jingnan Huang and his colleagues have recently observed that some behaviors of honeybees (such as foraging) are also motivated by a dopamine-based signaling process.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Studying late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century artifacts from an agricultural and domestic site in Texas, archaeologist Ayana O. Flewellen found that Black women employed as farm workers utilized hook-and-eye closures to fasten their clothes at the waist, giving themselves a silhouette similar to the one that was popular in contemporary fashion and typically achieved through more restrictive garments such as corsets.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Flewellen argues that this sartorial practice shows that these women balanced hegemonic ideals of femininity with the requirements of their physically demanding occupation.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In 2020, rap artist and professor A.D. Carson published the first peer-reviewed rap album about his experiences with Black masculinity called “i used to love to dream.”
cps.label: I

cps.text: Typically in peer review, experts evaluate scholarly articles prior to publication.
cps.label: I

cps.text: For Carson’s album, dubbed a “mixtap/e/ssay,” peer review involved both scholars and rap artists.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In combining elements of a mixtape album with scholarly essays that connect Carson’s lyrics to historical and contemporary contexts for listeners both inside and outside academia, Carson’s album helped redefine how scholarship is created and shared.
cps.label: C

cps.text: I went on with my day’s business tranquilly; but ever and anon vague suggestions kept wandering across my brain of reasons why I should quit Thornfield; and I kept involuntarily framing advertisements and pondering conjectures about new situations:
cps.label: C

cps.text: these thoughts I did not think to check; they might germinate and bear fruit if they could.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Astronomers are confident that the star Betelgeuse will eventually consume all the helium in its core and explode in a supernova.
cps.label: I

cps.text: They are much less confident, however, about when this will happen, since that depends on internal characteristics of Betelgeuse that are largely unknown.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Astrophysicist Sarafina El-Badry Nance and colleagues recently investigated whether acoustic waves in the star could be used to determine internal stellar states but concluded that this method could not sufficiently reveal Betelgeuse’s internal characteristics to allow its evolutionary state to be firmly fixed.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The following text is adapted from Herman Melville’s 1855 novel Israel Potter.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Israel is a young man wandering through New England during the late eighteenth century.
cps.label: I

cps.text: He hired himself out for three months; at the end of that time to receive for his wages two hundred acres of land lying in New Hampshire.
cps.label: I

cps.text: His employer proving false to the contract in the matter of the land, and there being no law in the country to force him to fulfil it, Israel—who, however brave-hearted, and even much of a dare-devil upon a pinch, seems nevertheless to have evinced, throughout many parts of his career, a singular patience and mildness—was obliged to look round for other means of livelihood than clearing out a farm for himself in the wilderness.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The following text is adapted from Herman Melville’s 1857 novel The Confidence-Man.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Years ago, a grave American savant, being in London, observed at an evening party there, a certain coxcombical fellow, as he thought, an absurd ribbon in his lapel, and full of smart [banter], whisking about to the admiration of as many as were disposed to admire.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Great was the savant’s disdain; but, chancing ere long to find himself in a corner with the jackanapes, got into conversation with him, when he was somewhat ill-prepared for the good sense of the jackanapes, but was altogether thrown aback, upon subsequently being [informed that he was] no less a personage than Sir Humphry Davy.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: In Jane Austen’s novel Mansfield Park, an almost imperceptible smile from potential suitor Henry Crawford causes the protagonist Fanny Price to blush; her embarrassment grows when she suspects that he is aware of it.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This moment—in which Fanny not only infers Henry’s mental state through his gestures, but also infers that he is drawing inferences about her mental state—illustrates what literary scholar George Butte calls “deep intersubjectivity,” a technique for representing interactions between consciousnesses through which Austen’s novels derive much of their social and psychological drama.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Lily had no real intimacy with nature, but she had a passion for the appropriate and could be keenly sensitive to a scene which was the fitting background of her own sensations.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The landscape outspread below her seemed an enlargement of her present mood, and she found something of herself in its calmness, its breadth, its long free reaches.
cps.label: C

cps.text: On the nearer slopes the sugar-maples wavered like pyres of light; lower down was a massing of grey orchards, and here and there the lingering green of an oak-grove.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Some studies have suggested that posture can influence cognition, but we should not overstate this phenomenon.
cps.label: C

cps.text: A case in point: In a 2014 study, Megan O’Brien and Alaa Ahmed had subjects stand or sit while making risky simulated economic decisions.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Standing is more physically unstable and cognitively demanding than sitting; accordingly, O’Brien and Ahmed hypothesized that standing subjects would display more risk aversion during the decision-making tasks than sitting subjects did, since they would want to avoid further feelings of discomfort and complicated risk evaluations.
cps.label: I

cps.text: But O’Brien and Ahmed actually found no difference in the groups’ performance.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Changes to vegetation cover and other human activities influence carbon and nitrogen levels in soil, though how deep these effects extend is unclear.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Hypothesizing that differences in land use lead to differences in carbon and nitrogen levels that are not restricted to the topsoil layer (0–30 cm deep), Chukwuebuka Okolo and colleagues sampled soils across multiple land-use types (e.g., grazing land, cropland, forest) within each of several Ethiopian locations.
cps.label: I

cps.text: They found, though, that across land-use types, carbon and nitrogen decreased to comparably low levels beyond depths of 30 cm.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Historians have argued that a crucial component of the Civil Rights Movement’s success in the 1960s was the Southern Christian Leadership Conference’s Citizen Education Program (CEP), which invited promising activists from across the South to its one-week training sessions in Dorchester, Georgia.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Led by experienced organizers such as Dorothy Cotton and Septima Clark, CEP attendees—more than 7,000 in all—participated in workshops on topics ranging from public speaking to legal doctrine before returning home and using their newly acquired knowledge to spearhead local civil rights initiatives.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A study by a team including finance professor Madhu Veeraraghavan suggests that exposure to sunshine during the workday can lead to overly optimistic behavior.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Using data spanning from 1994 to 2010 for a set of US companies, the team compared over 29,000 annual earnings forecasts to the actual earnings later reported by those companies.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The team found that the greater the exposure to sunshine at work in the two weeks before a manager submitted an earnings forecast, the more the manager’s forecast exceeded what the company actually earned that year.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Mathematician Claude Shannon is widely regarded as a foundational figure in information theory.
cps.label: I

cps.text: His most important paper, “A Mathematical Theory of Communication,” published in 1948 when he was employed at Bell Labs, utilized a concept called a “binary digit” (shortened to “bit”) to measure the amount of information in any signal and determine the fastest rate at which information could be transmitted while still being reliably decipherable.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Robert Gallagher, one of Shannon’s colleagues, said that the bit was “[Shannon’s] discovery, and from it the whole communications revolution has sprung.”
cps.label: C

cps.text: The following text is adapted from Zora Neale Hurston’s 1921 short story “John Redding Goes to Sea.”
cps.label: I

cps.text: John is a child who lives in a town in the woods.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Perhaps ten-year-old John was puzzling to the folk there in the Florida woods for he was an imaginative child and fond of day-dreams.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The St. John River flowed a scarce three hundred feet from his back door.
cps.label: I

cps.text: On its banks at this point grow numerous palms, luxuriant magnolias and bay trees.
cps.label: I

cps.text: On the bosom of the stream float millions of delicately colored hyacinths.
cps.label: I

cps.text: [John Redding] loved to wander down to the water’s edge, and, casting in dry twigs, watch them sail away down stream to Jacksonville, the sea, the wide world and [he] wanted to follow them.
cps.label: C

cps.text: A number of Indigenous politicians have been elected to the United States Congress since 2000 as members of the country’s two established political parties.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In Canada and several Latin American countries, on the other hand, Indigenous people have formed their own political parties to advance candidates who will advocate for the interests of their communities.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This movement has been particularly successful in Ecuador, where Guadalupe Llori, a member of the Indigenous party known as Pachakutik, was elected president of the National Assembly in 2021.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Several studies have found negligible electoral consequences for governments that impose fiscal austerity measures, yet some European governments recently suffered electorally due to their austerity programs.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Evelyne Huebscher and colleagues attribute this incongruity to governments’ tendency—not followed in the recent European cases—to implement austerity programs strategically to avoid electoral costs (e.g., setting spending cuts to take effect only after the next election),
cps.label: C

cps.text: which has obscured the inherent political risks of austerity measures in the election data scholars have examined.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Now the women began to test the trees—moving leisurely among them, axe in hand, and striking a single quick blow, to see if the sap would appear.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The trees, like people, have their individual characters; some were ready to yield up their life-blood, while others were more reluctant.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Now one of the birchen basins was set under each tree, and a hardwood chip driven deep into the cut which the axe had made.
cps.label: I

cps.text: From the corners of this chip—at first drop by drop, then more freely—the sap trickled into the little dishes.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Asteroid 6478 Gault has experienced intermittent mass loss since at least 2013, but in contrast to some other asteroids with repeated mass-loss episodes, 6478 Gault has not lost mass at its perihelion (the closest point of its orbit to the Sun), and thus the loss is not attributable to solar energy–driven ice vaporization.
cps.label: C

cps.text: And as Jane X. Luu et al. point out, the singular nature of impact ejection makes it untenable as an account of multiple loss episodes of similar duration over several years.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Instead, Luu et al. are likely correct that 6478 Gault is shedding mass due to rotational instability.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The following text is adapted from Jane Austen’s 1814 novel Mansfield Park.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The speaker, Tom, is considering staging a play at home with a group of his friends and family.
cps.label: I

cps.text: We mean nothing but a little amusement among ourselves, just to vary the scene, and exercise our powers in something new.
cps.label: C

cps.text: We want no audience, no publicity.
cps.label: C

cps.text: We may be trusted, I think, in choosing some play most perfectly unexceptionable; and I can conceive no greater harm or danger to any of us in conversing in the elegant written language of some respectable author than in chattering in words of our own.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Scholarly accounts of the Chicano movement—a movement that advocated for the social, political, and cultural empowerment of Mexican Americans and reached its zenith in the 1960s and 1970s—tend to focus on the most militant, outspoken figures in the movement, making it seem uniformly radical.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Geographer Juan Herrera has shown, however, that if we shift our focus toward the way the movement manifested in comparatively low-profile neighborhood institutions and projects, we see participants espousing an array of political orientations and approaches to community activism.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Raymond Antrobus, an accomplished poet and writer of prose, recently released his debut spoken word poetry album, The First Time I Wore Hearing Aids, in collaboration with producer Ian Brennan.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The album contains both autobiographical and reflective pieces combining Antrobus’s spoken words with Brennan’s fragmented audio elements and pieces of music to convey how people who are deaf may experience sound, both its presence and absence.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Some critics suggest that the album questions the function of sound in the world, highlighting that the experience of sound is multifaceted.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The mimosa tree evolved in East Asia, where the beetle Bruchidius terrenus preys on its seeds.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A group of ecologists led by Axel Mithöfer at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology in Germany examined the defensive responses of two varieties of the sweet potato ______ TN57, which is known for its insect resistance, and TN66, which is much more susceptible to pests.
cps.label: I

cps.text: With some 16,000 in attendance, the Second World Black and African Festival of Arts and ______ or FESTAC ‘77, as the event was more commonly known—became the largest pan-African event on record.
cps.label: I

cps.text: FESTAC drew people from around the world to Lagos, Nigeria, for a monthlong celebration of Black and African art, scholarship, and activism.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In modern plays, actors typically won’t acknowledge the ______ do so breaks the fourth wall, a metaphorical barrier between actors and audiences that allows viewers to suspend the knowledge that they’re watching a staged performance.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The relationship between genomes and epigenomes reveals how cells with identical DNA develop different ______
cps.label: I

cps.text: whereas the genome in each cell contains a complete DNA sequence, the epigenome consists of chemical compounds
cps.label: I

cps.text: that determine which traits in the sequence will be expressed.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Researchers studying magnetosensation have determined why some soil-dwelling roundworms in the Southern Hemisphere move in the opposite direction of Earth’s magnetic field when searching for ______.
cps.label: I

cps.text: in the Northern Hemisphere, the magnetic field points down, into the ground, but in the Southern Hemisphere, it points up, toward the surface and away from worms’ food sources.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Joshua Hinson, director of the language revitalization program of the Chickasaw Nation in Oklahoma, helped produce the world’s first Indigenous-language instructional app, Chickasaw ______ Chickasaw TV, in 2010;
cps.label: I

cps.text: and a Rosetta Stone language course in Chickasaw, in 2015.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Despite being cheap, versatile, and easy to produce, ______ they are made from nonrenewable petroleum, and most do not biodegrade in landfills.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In her 1983 book The Managed Heart: Commercialization of Human Feeling, sociologist Arlie Russell Hochschild first explored at length her conception of a “sociology of emotions”—the idea that the various cultural and ideological frameworks a person has internalized (class, gender, political affiliation, etc.) ______ each emotional reaction that person has within a situation.
cps.label: I

cps.text: American abstract artist Richard ______ his installations to make passersby keenly aware of how one’s movements are affected by the physical features of one’s environment,
cps.label: I

cps.text: assembles large-scale steel plates into sculptures that dominate the outdoor spaces they occupy.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Entomologists Yash Sondhi and Samuel Fabian have tried to explain why moths fly erratically around light sources at night.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Knowing that flying insects keep their backs pointed toward sunlight during the day, ______
cps.label: I

cps.text: Rabinal Achí is a precolonial Maya dance drama performed annually in Rabinal, a town in the Guatemalan highlands.
cps.label: I

cps.text: During the American Civil War, Thomas Morris Chester braved the front lines as a war correspondent for the Philadelphia Press.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Amplifying the voices and experiences of Black soldiers ______ of particular importance to Chester, who later became an activist and lawyer during the postwar Reconstruction period.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Working from an earlier discovery of Charpentier’s, chemists Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna—winners of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry—re-created and then reprogrammed the so-called “genetic scissors” of a species of DNA-cleaving bacteria.
cps.label: I

cps.text: ______ a tool that is revolutionizing the field of gene technology.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The artistic talents of Barbara Chase-Riboud, most known for her 1979 historical novel Sally Hemings and the conversation it inspired, ______ limited to the realm of prose:
cps.label: C

cps.text: she first excelled in sculpture, where her affinity for bronze—a material she described as “timeless” due to its use across eras and cultures—became part of her artistic identity.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In the 1970s, Janaki Ammal, a prominent botanist, emerged as a powerful voice in India’s environmental conservation movement.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Her exhaustive chromosomal survey of plants in Silent Valley, a pristine tropical forest in Kerala, India, that is home to nearly 1,000 species of native flora (many of which are endangered), ______ instrumental in the government’s decision to preserve the forest.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: In assessing the films of Japanese director Akira Kurosawa, ______ have missed his equally deep engagement with Japanese artistic traditions such as Noh theater.
cps.label: C

cps.text: When they were first discovered in Australia in 1798, duck-billed, beaver-tailed platypuses so defied categorization that one scientist assigned them the name Ornithorhynchus paradoxus: “paradoxical bird-snout.”
cps.label: I

cps.text: The animal, which lays eggs but also nurses ______ young with milk, has since been classified as belonging to the monotremes group.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Several advantages—the ability to react strongly with chip components, to avoid interference from other waves, and to be confined within tiny circuits—______ acoustic waves as a promising alternative to electrical waves for transmitting data on computer chips;
cps.label: I

cps.text: as a result, researchers are invested in developing more acoustic wave–based chips.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Known as Earth’s “living skin,” biocrusts are thin layers of soil held together by surface-dwelling microorganisms such as fungi, lichens, and cyanobacteria.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Fortifying soil in arid ecosystems against erosion, ______
cps.label: I

cps.text: Ten of William Shakespeare’s plays are classified as histories.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Although each one of these plays, which include Henry V and Richard III, ______ on a single historical figure (specifically, an English king), some, such as Henry VI Part One and Henry VI Part Two, feature different episodes from the same monarch’s life.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Woven from recycled yarn and hand tufted using a carpet weaving technique passed down by the artist’s Turkish grandmother,
cps.label: I

cps.text: ______ so lush and tactilely inviting that you are tempted to reach out and touch them.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In the canon of North African literature, Moroccan author Driss Chraïbi’s 1954 novel The Simple Past (Le Passé simple) looms large.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A coming-of-age story, a social meditation, and a sober gaze into the dark maw of French colonialism, ______ interrogates systemic power with memorable intensity.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Compared to that of alumina glass, ______ silica glass atoms are so far apart that they are unable to re-form bonds after being separated.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In 2016, engineer Vanessa Galvez oversaw the installation of 164 bioswales, vegetated channels designed to absorb and divert stormwater, along the streets of Queens, New York.
cps.label: I

cps.text: By reducing the runoff flowing into city sewers, ______
cps.label: I

cps.text: Planetary scientist Briony Horgan and her colleagues have determined that as much as 25 percent of the sand on Mars is composed of impact spherules.
cps.label: I

cps.text: These spherical bits of glass form when asteroids collide with the planet, ejecting bits of molten rock into the atmosphere that, after cooling and solidifying into glass, ______ back onto Mars’s surface.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Author Madeline L’Engle, ______ to create a suspenseful tone that draws the reader in, begins her novel A Wrinkle in Time
cps.label: C

cps.text: with descriptions of “wraithlike shadows” and “the frenzied lashing of the wind.”
cps.label: I

cps.text: A second-generation Japanese American, Wataru Misaka ______ in World War II (1941-45) and won two amateur national basketball championships at the University of Utah when he joined the New York Knicks for the 1947-48 season,
cps.label: I

cps.text: becoming the first non-white basketball player in the US’s top professional league.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Bengali author Toru Dutt’s A Sheaf Gleaned in French Fields (1876), a volume of English translations of French poems,
cps.label: I

cps.text: ______ scholars’ understanding of the transnational and multilingual contexts in which Dutt lived and worked.
cps.label: C

cps.text: In 2015, a team led by materials scientists Anirudha Sumant and Diana Berman succeeded in reducing the coefficient of friction (COF) between two surfaces to the lowest possible level—superlubricity.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A nearly frictionless (and, as its name suggests, extremely slippery) state, ______
cps.label: I

cps.text: In 1994, almost 200 years after the death of Wang Zhenyi, the International Astronomical ______ the contributions of the barrier-breaking 18th-century astronomer and author of “Dispute of the Procession of the Equinoxes,” naming a crater on Venus after her.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Researchers studying the “terra-cotta army,” the thousands of life-size statues of warriors found interred near the tomb of Emperor Qin Shi Huang of China, were shocked to realize that the shape of each statue’s ears, like the shape of each person’s ears, ______ unique.
cps.label: I

cps.text: In 1453, English King Henry VI became unfit to rule after falling gravely ill.
cps.label: I

cps.text: As a result, Parliament appointed Richard, Third Duke of York, who had a strong claim to the English throne, to rule as Lord Protector.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Upon recovering two years later, ______ forcing an angered Richard from the royal court and precipitating a series of battles later known as the Wars of the Roses.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: A model created by biologist Luis Valente predicts that the rate of speciation—the rate at which new species form—on an isolated island located approximately 5,000 kilometers from the nearest mainland ______ triple the rate of speciation on an island only 500 kilometers from the mainland.
cps.label: I

cps.text: A species of Byropsis algae produces toxins to avoid being eaten by predators.
cps.label: I

cps.text: However, in some cases, the toxins the organism uses to protect itself from predation actually ______ its attractiveness to predators.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The Hawaiian sea slug, for example, not only tolerates Byropsis toxins but actually uses them for protection in the same way the algae does.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The idea that time moves in only one direction is instinctively understood, yet it puzzles physicists.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Microbes are tiny organisms in the soil, water, and air all around us.
cps.label: I

cps.text: They thrive even in very harsh conditions.
cps.label: I

cps.text: That’s why Noah Fierer and colleagues were surprised when soil samples they collected from an extremely cold, dry area in Antarctica didn’t seem to contain any life.
cps.label: I

cps.text: The finding doesn’t prove that there are no microbes in that area, but the team says it does suggest that the environment severely restricts microbes’ survival.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Microbes are found in virtually every environment on Earth.
cps.label: I

cps.text: So it’s unlikely they would be completely absent from Fierer’s team’s study site, no matter how extreme the environment is.
cps.label: C

cps.text: There were probably so few organisms in the samples that current technology couldn’t detect them.
cps.label: C

cps.text: But since a spoonful of typical soil elsewhere might contain billions of microbes, the presence of so few in the Antarctic soil samples would show how challenging the conditions are.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Graphic novels are increasingly popular in bookstores and libraries, but they shouldn’t be classified as literature.
cps.label: C

cps.text: By definition, literature tells a story or conveys meaning through language only; graphic novels tell stories through illustrations and use language only sparingly, in captions and dialogue.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Graphic novels are experienced as series of images and not as language, making them more similar to film than to literature.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Graphic novels present their stories through both language and images.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Without captions and dialogue, readers would be unable to understand what is depicted in the illustrations: the story results from the interaction of text and image.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Moreover, Alison Bechdel’s Fun Home and many other graphic novels feature text that is as beautifully written as the prose found in many standard novels.
cps.label: I

cps.text: Therefore, graphic novels qualify as literary texts.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: In a study of the benefits of having free time, Marissa Sharif found that the reported sense of life satisfaction tended to plateau when participants had two hours of free time per day and actually began to fall when they had five hours of free time per day.
cps.label: I

cps.text: After further research, Sharif concluded that this dip in life satisfaction mainly occurred when individuals spent all their free time unproductively, such as by watching TV or playing games.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Psychologist James Maddux cautions against suggesting an ideal amount of free time.
cps.label: C

cps.text: The human desire for both free time and productivity is universal, but Maddux asserts that individuals have unique needs for life satisfaction.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Furthermore, he points out that there is no objective definition for what constitutes productivity; reading a book might be considered a productive activity by some, but idleness by others.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: Stage lighting theorist Adolphe Appia was perhaps the first to argue that light must be considered alongside all the various elements of a stage to create a single, unified performance.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Researcher Kelly Bremner, however, has noted that Appia lacked technical expertise in the use of light in the theater.
cps.label: C

cps.text: As a result of Appia’s inexperience, Bremner argues, Appia’s theory of light called for lighting practices that weren’t possible until after the advent of electricity around 1881.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Adolphe Appia was not an amateur in the practice of lighting.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Instead, it is precisely his exposure to lighting techniques at the time that contributed to his theory on the importance of light.
cps.label: C

cps.text: When working as an apprentice for a lighting specialist in his youth, Appia observed the use of portable lighting devices that could be operated by hand.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This experience developed his understanding of what was possible in the coordination of elements on the stage.
cps.label: CL

cps.text: The live music festival business is growing in event size and genre variety.
cps.label: I

cps.text: With so many consumer options, organizers are finding ways to cement festival attendance as a special experience worth sharing.
cps.label: I

cps.text: This phenomenon is linked to the growing “experiential economy,” where many find it gratifying to purchase lived experiences.
cps.label: I

cps.text: To ensure a profitable event, venues need to consider the overall consumer experience, not just the band lineup.
cps.label: C

cps.text: Music festival appearances are becoming a more important part of musicians’ careers.
cps.label: I

cps.text: One factor in this shift is the rising use of streaming services that allow access to huge numbers of songs for a monthly fee, subsequently reducing sales of full-length albums.
cps.label: I

cps.text: With this shift in consumer behavior, musicians are increasingly dependent on revenue from live performances.
cps.label: CL
